short.headline: India’s protectionist bet: imports drop, but jobs and exports haven’t followed
short.dek: India nearly doubled protective industrial policy measures after COVID. The World Bank’s new report shows the tariffs are cutting imports, but the bill falls on households, and the promised manufacturing jobs remain elusive.
short.body: India went from 125 to 239 new protective measures a year, the sixth‑most active country globally. Import restrictions work, they cut imports about 15% over three years, but export incentives show no clear effect. The sectors that get the most protection are high‑wage manufacturing, while services, which create the bulk of new jobs, receive almost none. The tariff wall costs every Indian household; modelling of proposed free trade deals with the EU and UK shows all income groups would gain from tariff cuts, rural poor most of all. Fiscal space is tight, implementation lags, and the flagship PLI scheme had disbursed only 12% of its funds by late 2025. The policy is a high‑stakes bet that has yet to deliver the manufacturing employment it was designed for.

macha.heading: Cool, so did India’s big protectionist push actually work?
macha.body: Look, the government threw the kitchen sink at protecting domestic industry after the pandemic — procurement, subsidies, tariffs, you name it. The raw count of new measures nearly doubled in four years. And yes, some of it is doing what it says on the tin: import restrictions are making foreign goods pricier and cutting imports. But the big promise of “atmanirbharta” was supposed to mean more Indian factories making things and creating steady jobs. On that score, the numbers are wobbling. The export incentives? We can’t even tell if they work; the evidence is just noise. And jobs? The industries getting the most armour are not the ones creating most new employment. Meanwhile, the ordinary household is quietly picking up the tab every time they buy something that costs more because of tariffs. The country is placing a huge, expensive bet, and the ledger so far says it has reduced imports but not produced the employment payoff.
macha.soWhat: India’s industrial policy surge is a costly gamble: the walls are up, but the jobs haven’t come, and the kitchen pays the bill.

article.title: Has industrial policy paid off for India?
article.standfirst: The country nearly doubled its use of protective measures after COVID. A World Bank report dissects who gets shielded, what the tariffs really cost, and why the manufacturing jobs didn’t appear. This article draws on the World Bank’s SAEU April 2026 report "Working with Industrial Policy."
article.bodyMarkdown:
How do you judge a policy that is popular everywhere but whose effects are stubbornly hard to pin down? India has bet heavily on industrial policy since the pandemic, and it is not a quiet bet. The country now introduces around 239 new protective measures a year, up from 125 before COVID, placing it among the most active protectors in the world. This article works through the evidence from the World Bank’s SAEU April 2026 report "Working with Industrial Policy", asking the blunt questions: does any of this work, for whom, and at what cost?

## How much has India’s use of protective industrial policy really grown?

In the four years after the pandemic (2022‑25), India averaged 239.3 new protective measures annually, nearly double the 124.8 it averaged in 2016‑19. A protective measure is anything that gives domestic firms an edge over foreign ones: an import ban, a local‑content rule for government purchases, a cash subsidy to domestic producers. By this count, India is an industrial‑policy giant. Its neighbours barely register on the same scale. Bangladesh introduced 12 measures a year in 2022‑25, Sri Lanka 9, Nepal 2.8, and Bhutan 0.3. You are looking at a country that has weaponised state purchasing and subsidy budgets to an extent its South Asian peers have not. But the counting rule is important: every measure counts as one, whether it is a sweeping import ban or a tiny tweak to a tax break. That flattens the real money behind each intervention into a simple count.

## Is India alone in this protectionist turn?

No. The whole world is doing it too. In 2010, countries introduced 5,953 new industrial policy measures globally. By 2025, that figure had risen to 9,171. Protective measures, the ones that shield domestic producers from import competition, grew even faster, from 4,241 in 2010 to 7,230 last year. The surge began well before COVID, but the pandemic poured petrol on it. Advanced economies, in particular, started intervening at a scale that would have been unthinkable a generation ago. India’s surge, in other words, is riding a powerful global wave. It is not an outlier; it is one of the bigger surfers on it.

## How does India rank among the big protectionist players?

Put the raw counts side by side and India sits in sixth place globally, behind the United States (746.5 measures per year in 2022‑25), China (725.5), Brazil (339.3), Italy (291.3) and Germany (267.8). Among emerging economies, only China and Brazil are more active. India’s 239.3 measures a year is nearly double what it was before 2020, while some other big users like Canada actually became less active. Raw counts, however, do not tell you how much economic weight each measure carries. An import restriction in the United States covers a far larger market than one in India. So the ranking gives you the volume of the protectionist drumbeat, not the decibel level.

## What tools does India use to protect its industries?

India’s playbook looks very different from the rest of South Asia. In Sri Lanka, 77.8% of all protective measures are import restrictions. In Nepal, the figure is 54.5%. In India, import restrictions account for only 22.5% of the total. Public procurement, where the government uses its own buying power to favour local firms, makes up 22.8% of India’s measures, compared to near zero in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal. Subsidies are the largest slice at 29.7%. The Indian state is a massive buyer, with government procurement spending at roughly 20% of GDP, more than twice the median for emerging economies. That is how Delhi turns a shopping list into an industrial policy: when the government decides to buy Indian steel, Indian cement or Indian electronics, it can reshape entire supply chains without touching a single tariff rate.

## Which kind of industries does India choose to protect?

Not dying ones. The stereotype of protectionism defending uncompetitive sunset industries does not hold for India. The World Bank’s analysis shows that protection flows to sectors with higher import competition, a one‑percentage‑point rise in a sector’s import share predicts 0.47 more protective measures, which is a strong and statistically significant relationship. But it also flows to exporting sectors (coefficient 0.39) and, in manufacturing, to sectors that pay higher hourly wages (0.24), have larger firms by employment (0.21) and are more productive (0.15). The Indian state is not propping up the old; it is backing the strong, betting that a little extra shelter will turn competitive firms into world‑class ones. The catch is that these are correlations, not proof that the policies themselves caused those sectors to be high‑wage or productive.

## Which specific sectors get the most protection?

About half of all protective industrial policy measures target manufacturing, even though manufacturing accounts for only about 14% of South Asian employment. Within manufacturing, food processing still claims the largest share, 7.5% of protective measures in 2022‑25, but that share has fallen from 11.9% in 2016‑19. The big riser is electronics, which has jumped to 6.6% of measures in the last few years, a direct reflection of the production‑linked incentive schemes and the broader push to make India an electronics manufacturing hub. Other heavily protected sectors include civil engineering (5.7%), basic metals (5.4%) and chemicals (5.4%). The shift from food to electronics is the story of India’s industrial policy in the 2020s, moving from the shop floor of the past to the ambitions of the future.

## How high is India’s tariff wall compared to the world?

India’s average applied import duty is 15.8%. That is nearly double the emerging‑economy median of 8.5% and roughly triple the 25th percentile of 5.6%. Only Sri Lanka, once you include its para‑tariffs, is higher in the region at 19%. In Bangladesh, the figure is 14%. A simple average like this masks enormous variation, some goods face duties well over 100% while many inputs are duty‑free, but it tells you what the typical importer bumps into. India is not quietly nudging the tariff dial; it has built a wall that is among the steepest in any large economy.

## Do India’s trade defence measures actually cut imports?

The honest answer is half yes, half we cannot tell. Import‑restricting measures, anti‑dumping duties, safeguards, outright import bans, do reduce imports. After three years, the cumulative decline is about 15%, though the confidence band is wide, with the possible effect ranging from a 28% drop to a 49% increase. That uncertainty is what trade data looks like: real, but noisy. Export incentives are a different story. After four years, the estimated effect on exports is actually negative at −7.6%, but the confidence interval stretches from −51.2% to +87.3%. That range includes both a large boost and a large collapse. Statistically, we simply cannot say whether these export promotions work. If you are spending public money on them, that should worry you.

## Has the protection push created jobs where it matters?

The payoff in jobs is nearly invisible. In India, the non‑agricultural sectors that received the fewest industrial policy measures, mostly services, grew employment at 0.91% a year. The sectors that received the most protection grew at 0.95% a year. The difference is trivial. The country’s great job machine of the past decade has been services, which got almost no targeted industrial policy support. In Bangladesh, by contrast, the least‑protected non‑farm sectors grew employment at 4.26% a year, a transformational pace. The data covers only formal‑sector workers, so if manufacturing has surged in informal employment, this picture could change, but from what the formal numbers show, the protection wall did not produce a noticeable jobs bump.

## Who pays the bill for the protectionist wall?

You do. Every Indian household, across every income level. The World Bank modelled what would happen if the proposed free trade agreements with the European Union and the United Kingdom were in place and the tariff cuts they would bring took effect. The answer is that every single household gains in consumption. Rural households gain more than urban ones. The poorest rural quintile gains 0.33%, as does the richest rural quintile. Urban households gain between 0.24% and 0.26%. These are not large numbers, we are talking about a fraction of a percent of a family’s monthly spending, but the direction is unanimous. A tariff is a tax, and when you lower it, households keep more of what they earn. The protection wall India has built is paid for quietly, every day, at the kitchen table.

## Do lower tariffs really help the poor the most?

Yes. Real income effects mirror the consumption story. Tariff cuts raise real income for every household, and again rural families gain proportionately more. The poorest rural quintile sees a 0.22% increase in real income; the richest urban quintile, 0.19%. Why do the poor gain more? Poorer households spend a larger share of their budget on traded goods, food, clothing, basic durables, and those are exactly the products that bear heavier tariffs in India today. Removing the tariff is like giving a small, permanent tax cut that is tilted toward those who can least afford the existing burden. The caveat is that these are static first‑order estimates; they assume tariff cuts fully pass through to consumer prices and do not count the possibility that more exports could raise wages or attract investment.

## Can India afford its industrial policy ambitions?

The fiscal maths is tight. India’s tax revenue averaged 18% of GDP between 2019 and 2023, below the emerging‑economy average of 20.4%. In South Asia, only the Maldives (20.1%) and Nepal (18.6%) collect more; Bangladesh (8.5%) and Sri Lanka (10%) collect far less. Government debt is already above the EMDE average. Into this constrained space, India has loaded ambitious spending programmes. The production‑linked incentive scheme, the flagship of the industrial policy push, had disbursed only about 12% of its allocated funds by September 2025, held back by bureaucratic hurdles and inter‑ministerial coordination problems. You can announce a policy in Delhi, but getting the money out the door and into a factory floor is a different exercise entirely.

## Can India’s infrastructure keep up with the policy intent?

Even well‑designed industrial policy hits a wall if it takes weeks to clear goods through customs. For a medium‑sized Indian firm, clearing an import takes about 16.3 days, and an export takes about 19.9 days. The typical emerging‑economy firm clears imports in 5.1 days and exports in 5.3 days. That is a three to fourfold gap. Even in South Asia, Bangladesh manages in 8.9 days both ways, and Nepal gets it done in 4 to 4.5 days. A factory that waits nearly three weeks for a shipment of components faces a hidden tax on every order, a tax that no tariff schedule captures but that can erase the advantage of any subsidy or local procurement preference. The design of industrial policy in Delhi often meets its match in a customs shed in Mumbai.

## Is India’s government machinery capable of executing this strategy?

On paper, India’s bureaucracy is good by the standards of emerging economies. The World Bank’s government effectiveness index places India in the 67.9th percentile globally, well above the EMDE median of 37.3. Only Bhutan (69.3) rates higher in South Asia. But the index also reveals the delivery gap. The advanced‑economy median sits at the 88th percentile. That twenty‑point gap between India’s state capacity and that of a typical rich country is where many industrial policies slow down. Complex interventions, production‑linked incentives, phased manufacturing programmes, sector‑specific tax breaks, demand a civil service that can coordinate across ministries, review outcomes, cut dead programmes, and resist capture. India’s government has the design skills; the execution is often what falls short.

## Isn’t India opening up even as it builds protectionist walls?

Yes. The story of the last five years is not only about protection. While India was putting up new defensive measures, it was also negotiating its largest ever free trade agreements. The deals with the European Union and the United Kingdom, once in force, will roughly double the share of global output India has preferential market access to: from a current 15.5% to around 33% (adding the 17.5% of concluded but not yet in force agreements). That would push India ahead of China (30.3%), Turkey (26.8%) and Brazil (3.7%) in FTA coverage. The two strategies, building walls and opening doors, exist in tension. India is betting that the time bought by the walls allows its industries to get strong enough to walk through the doors, but the walls also make the doors harder to open fully.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Government actions that try to shape which industries grow, by protecting them from foreign competition, giving them subsidies, or buying their products. Think of it as the state picking and backing its champion sectors.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The entire page asks whether India’s version has paid off.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Any new government rule or action that gives domestic firms an advantage over foreign ones. This includes raising import duties, banning certain imports, requiring government agencies to buy local, or giving cash subsidies only to Indian producers. The key caveat: the database counts every such action equally, whether it is a sweeping import ban or a tiny tweak to a tax break.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: All the surge numbers in this article come from this counting rule, so one measure is not necessarily equal in impact to another.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A large public database that tracks government policy changes affecting international trade. Researchers use it to count how many new protective measures each country introduces each year.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The entire surge narrative rests on this dataset, and its equal-counting rule is a crucial caveat.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Emerging market and developing economies. These are countries that are not yet fully wealthy but are not the poorest either. India, China, Brazil and Bangladesh are examples. Advanced economies (AEs) are the rich ones like the US, Germany and Japan.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Comparisons between India and the EMDE median ground the story in peer context.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Free trade agreement: a deal between countries to reduce tariffs on each other’s goods. Imagine a special market access card that lets your goods enter a partner’s country at a lower tax rate than goods from outsiders.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India’s FTAs with the EU and UK are the counterweight to its protectionist surge.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The actual tax rate a country charges on incoming goods at the border. It is often lower than the maximum rate it has promised at the WTO. It is what a real importer pays, right now.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The 15.8% figure is India’s applied duty, the price wall its industrial policy puts between Indian consumers and foreign goods.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: When the government buys goods or services. From roads and bridges to stationery and laptops, the government is a massive shopper. Industrial policy turns that shopping list into a tool: prefer local suppliers, even if they are more expensive.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India’s distinctive use of procurement — 22.8% of its protective measures — sets it apart from neighbours.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A government scheme that pays a cash bonus to manufacturers based on how much they produce. It is like a reward for making things in India, designed to attract big factories and global supply chains.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The PLI is India’s flagship industrial policy for electronics and other high-tech sectors, but it had disbursed only about 12% of its budget by September 2025.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A number that shows whether a country exports more of a product than the world average. A positive RCA means the country is relatively good at making that thing and sells a lot of it abroad.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The FTA tariff-cut chart could use RCA to see if India is committing to bigger tariff cuts in sectors where it is already strong or weak, but this specific chart is not included in the final article set.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A World Bank score that measures how well the state machinery works: whether civil servants are competent, rules are predictable, and policies actually get implemented. A high score means the government can get things done.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India’s 67.9 percentile score shows its bureaucracy is decent, but the gap to rich countries (88th) is where industrial policy stumbles.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A range around a statistical estimate that tells you how uncertain the number is. A wide interval means the true effect could be very different from the central estimate; a narrow one means we are fairly sure.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The export incentive effect has a confidence band from -51.2% to +87.3%, meaning we cannot say whether it works.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A number that shows how much one thing changes when another thing goes up by one unit. For example, a coefficient of 0.47 on import share means that a 1-percentage-point higher import share predicts 0.47 more protective measures.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Used to show what drives India’s targeting of industries.

chartExplainers.title: India nearly doubled its protective industrial policy measures
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s annual new protective measures jumped from 125 to 239, far outstripping other South Asian countries.
chartExplainers.detail: The chart compares the annual average number of new protective industrial policy measures for South Asian countries in two periods: 2016‑19 and 2022‑25. India’s count rose from 124.8 to 239.3, nearly doubling. Bangladesh, the next most active, introduced only 12 per year in the later period, up from 2.8. Sri Lanka increased from 14.5 to 9, Nepal from 1.3 to 2.8, and Bhutan and Maldives barely register. Each measure is an action that favours domestic firms over foreign competitors — an import ban, a subsidy, a local procurement rule. The visual directly answers the question of the page by showing the scale and speed of India’s protective turn.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This is the headline chart. It gives the raw scale of the surge and contextualises India against its neighbours.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare the bar lengths between the two periods for each country; the focus is India’s sharp jump.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not treat every measure as equal in effect: a broad import ban and a minor tweak to a subsidy programme count the same in this tally.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use horizontal bars with clean labels and large, sparse tick marks for easy phone reading.

chartExplainers.title: The world is doing it too — a global protectionist wave
chartExplainers.takeaway: Total new industrial policy measures worldwide rose from 5,953 to 9,171, driven mainly by protective actions.
chartExplainers.detail: This line chart tracks the global count of new industrial policy interventions from 2010 to 2025. Two lines are shown: total measures and protective measures. Both series rise gently until about 2018 and then accelerate sharply. The protective line dominates, climbing from 4,241 in 2010 to 7,230 in 2025. That means most new industrial policy in the world is about shielding domestic firms from imports. India’s own surge is not an isolated move; it is part of a worldwide shift that intensified after the pandemic, with advanced economies leading the charge.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Essential context: India is not an outlier but a large participant in a global trend.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Watch the two lines as they climb: the gap between total and protective narrows, meaning almost all the new activity is protectionist.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not mistake this global total for an average per country; many small economies add few measures while a few large ones dominate.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A single line chart with large labels and sparse annual ticks works well on a phone screen.

chartExplainers.title: Where India sits among the big protectionist players
chartExplainers.takeaway: India ranks sixth globally in protective industrial policy measures, with 239 per year, behind the US, China, Brazil, Italy and Germany.
chartExplainers.detail: The chart lists the top countries by annual average new protective measures in 2022‑25. The United States leads with 746.5 measures, China follows at 725.5, Brazil at 339.3, Italy at 291.3, Germany at 267.8, and then India at 239.3. To give the pre‑COVID baseline, the chart also shows the 2016‑19 averages: India’s then was 124.8, so the surge is clear. Among emerging economies, India is third. The visual lets you place India’s protectionist push in global terms, though raw counts don’t reflect the economic weight of each measure.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Shows India’s standing: major league but not the biggest, and highlights the jump.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare India’s bar length to the US and China; note the thin bar for 2016‑19 to see the acceleration.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read rank as economic consequence. A measure by the US may affect a larger market than one by India.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Horizontal bars with a secondary thinner bar for the earlier period. Keep labels short.

chartExplainers.title: India’s toolkit: procurement and subsidies, not just tariffs
chartExplainers.takeaway: India uses import restrictions for only 22.5% of its protective measures, far less than Sri Lanka’s 77.8%, and leans heavily on procurement (22.8%) and subsidies (29.7%).
chartExplainers.detail: A stacked‑bar chart breaks down the composition of protective measures into five instrument categories for India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal in 2022‑25. India’s largest share is subsidies (29.7%), followed by import restrictions (22.5%), procurement (22.8%), exports (10.9%) and other (14.2%). In contrast, Sri Lanka relies on imports for 77.8% of its measures, and Nepal 54.5%. Public procurement is virtually absent in Bangladesh and Sri Lanka and modest in Nepal. The chart reveals that India’s industrial policy is executed as much through the government’s cheque book and purchasing power as through border taxes.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This visual reveals India’s distinctive instrument mix, explaining why its industrial policy is more than tariff‑based.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar is a country; the coloured segments show the share of instruments. Look at the tiny import‑restriction share in India compared to Sri Lanka.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume a measure’s share equals its fiscal cost. A single procurement contract can be worth far more than many smaller tariff adjustments.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Stacked bars with clear colour legend and short labels work well on a phone.

chartExplainers.title: Who India protects: high-wage sectors and large firms
chartExplainers.takeaway: Higher import penetration, wages, firm size and productivity all predict more protective measures in India.
chartExplainers.detail: This horizontal‑bar chart displays regression coefficients showing which sector characteristics predict more protective industrial policy in India (2022‑25). The import share coefficient is 0.47, meaning a one‑percentage‑point higher import share predicts 0.47 more measures. Export share (0.39), hourly wages in manufacturing (0.24), firm employment size (0.21) and firm productivity (0.15) are all positive and statistically significant. chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Counters the stereotype that industrial policy is for declining sectors; India targets the strong.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar is a coefficient; taller bars mean the factor is a stronger predictor. Confidence intervals show uncertainty.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These are correlations, not proof that the policies caused the sector traits. Reverse causality is possible.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use horizontal bars with whiskers. A phone‑friendly note explaining coefficients can help.

chartExplainers.detail: This grouped‑bar chart shows annual employment growth by industrial policy intensity quartile for India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. In India, the lowest quartile (sectors with the fewest protective measures — mostly services) grew at 0.91% a year, while the middle quartiles grew at 0.95%. The difference is trivial. By contrast, Bangladesh’s lowest‑protection sectors exploded at 4.26% a year. The chart exposes a disconnect: the heavy protective armour goes to manufacturing, but the jobs engine remains services, which receives almost no targeted policy support.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It visualises the core disappointment: the protection push didn’t shift the employment needle.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare the bar for lowest‑quartile India with the middle‑quartile India; they are nearly equal. Then contrast with Bangladesh’s lowest quartile.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These are formal‑sector jobs only. Manufacturing may have large informal employment not captured here.

chartExplainers.title: The hidden tax: tariffs hurt Indian households
chartExplainers.takeaway: Every Indian household would gain in consumption from the EU/UK FTA tariff cuts, with the rural poor gaining the most (0.33%).
chartExplainers.detail: A horizontal‑bar chart shows the modelled consumption effects of tariff cuts under the proposed EU and UK free trade agreements for different income quintiles in rural and urban India. All bars are positive. Rural households gain 0.31‑0.33%, with the poorest quintile (Q1) and the richest (Q5) both gaining 0.33%. Urban households gain 0.24‑0.26%. The uniformity of the gain and the slight pro‑poor tilt make the point: tariffs are a regressive tax, and reducing them helps every family, with the biggest lift going to those who spend the largest share of their budget on traded goods.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Puts a human face on the cost of protectionism, showing who bears the burden of the tariff wall.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Look at the rural bars: all are higher than urban ones, and Q1 and Q5 are near the top. The pattern confirms that tariff cuts help everyone.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These are static gains; they assume full pass‑through of tariff cuts to prices and exclude potential wage or export effects.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Horizontal bars with labels like 'Rural Q1', 'Urban Q1', grouped by area.

chartExplainers.title: Real incomes rise too, especially for the poorest
chartExplainers.takeaway: Tariff cuts raise real incomes across all households, with rural Q1 gaining 0.22% and urban Q1 0.16%.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart echoes the consumption finding but uses real income, a measure of purchasing power. Every quintile shows a positive effect. Rural gains are again larger: the poorest rural quintile gets a 0.22% increase, the richest rural quintile 0.24%. Urban gains range from 0.16% to 0.19%. The pattern strengthens the earlier result: lower tariffs make the average Indian household slightly better off in real terms, and the poorest benefit proportionately more. Tariffs act like a sales tax on everyday life, and removing them is a net positive for those who feel price rises most.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Confirms the consumption story with a different metric, reinforcing that tariffs are regressive.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Same structure: rural bars longer, poorest quintiles among the longest. All positive.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: As with consumption, these are static estimates; they don’t model employment or productivity gains.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Horizontal bars, replicate the style of the previous chart for comparability.

chartExplainers.title: Fiscal space is tight
chartExplainers.takeaway: India collects 18% of GDP in tax revenue, below the EMDE average of 20.4%.
chartExplainers.detail: A bar chart compares South Asian countries and the EMDE average for tax revenue as a share of GDP, averaged over 2019‑23. India stands at 18%, below the EMDE average line of 20.4% and below Nepal (18.6%) and Maldives (20.1%). Bangladesh (8.5%) and Sri Lanka (10%) are far lower. With government debt above the EMDE average and the flagship PLI scheme having disbursed only about 12% of its allocated funds by late 2025, the tight fiscal space limits how much extra protectionist spending the state can realistically absorb.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Highlights the financial constraint on India’s industrial policy ambitions.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Look at the dashed EMDE average line; India’s bar falls below it.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Tax‑to‑GDP is an average over five years; recent reforms might have nudged it, but not dramatically.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Horizontal bars with a reference line, clear country labels.

chartExplainers.title: Customs clearance: India takes 3–4 times longer than EMDE peers
chartExplainers.takeaway: Medium‑sized Indian firms take about 16 days to clear imports and 20 days to clear exports, vs an EMDE median of about 5 days.
chartExplainers.detail: The chart uses bars to show customs clearance times in days for imports and exports across South Asian countries against the EMDE median. India’s import clearance takes 16.3 days, exports 19.9 days. The EMDE medians are 5.1 and 5.3 days respectively. Bangladesh clears both in 8.9 days, Bhutan in 5.5 and 6, Nepal in 4 and 4.5. India’s logistics friction is a severe non‑tariff barrier: a factory waiting three weeks for components bears an inventory cost that no subsidy can fully offset. Implementation on the ground often undoes the intent designed in the capital.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Illustrates the non‑tariff barriers that undercut industrial policy incentives.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Note India’s tall bars vs the small EMDE median dots; the time gap is a hidden tax on trade.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Survey data, so actual times can vary by port, product and firm size.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Horizontal bars with import/export side‑by‑side per country and a dashed median line.

chartExplainers.title: Government effectiveness: India scores well, but far behind advanced economies
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s 67.9 percentile is strong for an EMDE (median 37.3) but a long way from the advanced‑economy median of 88.
chartExplainers.detail: A bar chart of government effectiveness percentile ranks for South Asian countries in 2024. India scores 67.9, just below Bhutan at 69.3 and well above the EMDE median of 37.3. Maldives (45), Sri Lanka (40), Bangladesh (30) and Nepal (20) all trail. While India’s civil service appears capable by EMDE standards, the gap to the typical rich‑country score (88th percentile) represents the delivery deficit. Complex industrial policies require sustained coordination, monitoring and periodic pruning — tasks that push bureaucratic capacity to its limits.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Contextualises the implementation gap; India’s bureaucracy is decent, but not rich‑world class.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare India’s bar to the EMDE median line; the real story is the distance between India’s bar and the implied AE median.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The index reflects general bureaucratic quality, not specific industrial policy capacity.

chartExplainers.title: India is also opening up: FTA coverage set to double
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s current FTA coverage of 15.5% of global GDP will rise to 33% when concluded EU and UK deals are in force.
chartExplainers.detail: This horizontal‑bar chart shows the share of global GDP covered by free trade agreements for several emerging economies, split between current and concluded agreements. India’s current coverage is 15.5%, but it has 17.5% worth of concluded FTAs not yet in force, bringing the total to about 33%. That would surpass China (30.3%), Turkey (26.8%) and Brazil (3.7%). While India has been building tariff walls, it has also been negotiating historic market access deals. The two strategies exist in tension, but the data show the doors are swinging open alongside the walls.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The counterweight to the protection story; India isn’t only raising barriers.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Look at the stacked or adjacent bars: current (lighter) plus concluded (darker) gives the future total. India’s combined bar is larger than China’s.

editorialPlanDraft.answerThesis: India’s protective industrial policy surge is a high-stakes bet that has cut imports but has not yet delivered jobs or export gains, while quietly taxing households and straining fiscal capacity.
requiredConcepts: India nearly doubled its annual average of new protective industrial policy measures between the four years before COVID (2016-19, about 125 a year) and the four years after (2022-25, about 239 a year). This made India the sixth-most-active country globally in protective industrial policy and the third-most-active emerging economy, behind only China and Brazil

This was not a uniquely Indian move. Industrial policy has surged worldwide since the pandemic, with the total number of new measures roughly doubling across both advanced economies and EMDEs. India is surfing a global wave, but it is a bigger wave than most

India's playbook is distinctive. Unlike Sri Lanka, where 78% of protective measures are import restrictions, or Nepal at 55%, India uses import restrictions for only about 23% of its measures. Instead, India relies heavily on public procurement (about 23% of measures, versus near-zero in the rest of South Asia) and subsidies (about 30%). Government procurement spending in India is about 20% of GDP, more than twice the EMDE median of 8%. The Indian state is using its massive purchasing power as its main industrial policy tool

Contrary to the stereotype of protecting uncompetitive sunset industries, India directs more industrial policy at manufacturing sectors with higher average wages and larger, more productive firms. Protected manufacturing sectors pay about 30% higher wages than unprotected ones, and the firms in them are about 100% larger by employment and 40% more productive. India is betting on upgrading, not preserving

The policy flows to where import competition is highest. A one-percentage-point increase in a sector's import share predicts 0.47 more protective measures in India — a strong and statistically significant relationship. Export-oriented sectors also get more protection, suggesting the measures are dual-purpose rather than purely defensive

About half of all protective industrial policy measures target manufacturing, even though manufacturing accounts for only about 14% of South Asian employment. Within manufacturing, food processing is still the largest beneficiary, but electronics has surged to second place in the 2020s, reflecting India's production-linked incentive schemes and the broader push into high-tech manufacturing

India's average applied import duty of about 15.8% is roughly double the EMDE median of 8.5% and about triple the 25th percentile. Only Sri Lanka, with its additional para-tariffs on top of statutory duties, is higher in the region at about 19%

The scorecard on whether these policies work is mixed. Import-restricting measures (anti-dumping duties, safeguards, import bans) do reduce imports significantly — by about 15% after three years — though with wide confidence intervals. Export-promoting measures (export subsidies, tax incentives) show no statistically significant effect on exports. The confidence band spans both positive and negative territory, meaning we simply cannot tell if they work from the available data

The employment payoff is barely visible. In India, the non-agricultural sectors that received the fewest industrial policy measures — mostly services — grew employment at about 0.91% a year. The sectors that received the most protection grew at about 0.95% a year. The difference is trivial. The vast majority of job creation in India over the past decade came from services, which received almost no targeted industrial policy support

The protection wall is paid for at the kitchen table. The World Bank's modelling of India's proposed free trade agreements with the European Union and the United Kingdom shows that the tariff cuts would raise consumption for every single household, across all income levels. Rural households would gain 0.20 to 0.33% in consumption; urban households 0.16 to 0.26%. The poorest rural quintile gains the most. Real income effects are also universally positive. Tariffs are a regressive tax on Indian consumers

India's fiscal capacity to sustain an ambitious industrial policy is stretched. Tax revenue at about 18% of GDP lags the EMDE average of 20.4%, and is below every other South Asian country except Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. Government debt is above the EMDE average. The flagship Production-Linked Incentive scheme, a centrepiece of India's industrial policy, had disbursed only about 12% of its allocated funds as of September 2025, held back by bureaucratic hurdles and inter-ministerial coordination problems

Implementation capacity is the binding constraint. It takes medium-sized Indian firms about 16 days to clear imports through customs and about 20 days to clear exports — roughly three to four times the EMDE medians of about five days. India's government effectiveness ranks in the 68th percentile globally, good for an EMDE but well below the advanced-economy median of the 88th percentile. The design of industrial policy in Delhi often runs into the reality of a customs shed in Mumbai

The counterweight to the protection surge is that India is simultaneously negotiating its largest-ever free trade agreements. The deals with the EU and UK, once in force, will double the share of global output India has preferential access to — from about 16% to about 33%. This would put India ahead of China, Turkey and Brazil in FTA coverage. India is not only building walls; it is opening doors, and the two strategies exist in tension

The electronics sector is the bright spot the World Bank holds up. Coordinated policies — the National Policy on Electronics, production-linked incentives, and plug-and-play industrial parks in Tamil Nadu — have attracted more than 4 billion US dollars in foreign direct investment, brought Apple suppliers to Indian soil, and driven a boom in mobile phone exports. It is the proof of concept. But it is the exception, not the rule, and it required unusually well-coordinated policy across multiple arms of government

Honesty caveats to state plainly: the policy measure counts come from the Global Trade Alert database and treat a sweeping import ban the same as a minor subsidy tweak — they measure quantity, not size or monetary value. The employment data covers only the formal sector. The trade impulse responses have wide confidence intervals, especially for export incentives. The FTA household effects are static first-order estimates that assume full pass-through of tariff cuts to consumer prices and do not include second-order gains from export expansion or FDI. The regression results show correlations, not causal proof. And the data end in 2023-2025, so the most recent policy shifts — including the 2026 US tariff escalation and India's responses — are not captured

chartPlan.whyShowThis: Quantifies the barrier in a single comparable number: India’s 15.8% vs the EMDE median 8.5%.
chartPlan.howToRead: Compare India’s bar to the EMDE median and Sri Lanka’s; note that Sri Lanka’s includes para-tariffs.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: A simple average hides extreme peaks; some products face duties exceeding 100% while many inputs are duty-free.

chartPlan.title: Trade defence cuts imports. Export incentives? Not so much.
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The policy scorecard: imports fall after trade defence, but export incentives show no significant effect.
chartPlan.howToRead: Watch the two lines from year 0. The import line dips, but the export line bounces around zero within a wide confidence band.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Confidence bands are broad—do not read the point estimates as precise; the export effect is statistically insignificant.

chartPlan.title: The jobs paradox: services create jobs but get no protection
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Visualizes the disconnect between where protection goes and where jobs are created.
chartPlan.howToRead: Compare employment growth across IP quartiles; the lowest-protection sectors (mostly services) grew almost as fast as the most-protected in India.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: These are formal-sector jobs only; manufacturing has a large informal workforce not in this data, which could shift the picture.

chartPlan.title: The hidden tax: tariffs hurt Indian households
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Puts a human face on the cost: every household gains when tariffs are cut, with the rural poor gaining most.
chartPlan.howToRead: Check the bars for rural vs urban quintiles; all are positive, rural Q1 gets 0.33%.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: These are static gains; they do not include possible wage increases from export growth, which could change the distribution.

chartPlan.title: Real incomes rise too, especially for the poorest
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Confirms the consumption story using real income, reinforcing that tariff cuts are pro-poor.
chartPlan.howToRead: Similar pattern: rural gains larger than urban, poorer quintiles gain proportionately more.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Real income effects are also static; they do not model employment or productivity effects from increased trade.

chartPlan.title: Fiscal space is tight
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Shows India’s limited tax base relative to its industrial policy ambitions.
chartPlan.howToRead: Compare India’s 18% to the EMDE average of 20.4%; note that all South Asian countries except Maldives are below the EMDE average.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Tax-to-GDP is an average over 2019-23; recent reforms may have nudged it, but not dramatically.

chartPlan.title: Customs clearance: India takes 3–4 times longer than EMDE peers
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Illustrates the non-tariff barriers that undercut industrial policy incentives.
chartPlan.howToRead: Note India’s 16-20 days vs the EMDE median of ~5 days; even other South Asian countries clear faster.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Survey data, so actual times may vary by port, product, and firm size.

chartPlan.title: Government effectiveness: India scores well, but far behind advanced economies
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Contextualizes the implementation gap: India’s bureaucracy is good by EMDE standards, but the gap to AE median is the delivery deficit.
chartPlan.howToRead: Compare India’s percentile (68th) to EMDE median (37th) and the implied AE median (~88th).
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Government effectiveness is a broad index; it does not capture sector-specific capacity to manage industrial policy.

chartPlan.title: India is also opening up: FTA coverage set to double
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The counterbalance: India’s protectionism co-exists with a historic opening through FTAs.
chartPlan.howToRead: Look at India’s current (15.5%) plus concluded (17.5%) vs EMDE median (18.6%); note it would surpass China.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Concluded does not mean in force; ratification and implementation could delay or reduce the effective coverage.

visualizationDecisions.reason: Comparing a short pre- and post-COVID snapshot makes the surge instantly readable on a phone.
A decade-plus trend with a sharp post-2019 inflection needs a line chart to show the wave.
Ranking countries is clearest with bars; adding the 2016-19 average as a thinner bar for comparison.
Showing the composition of tools within each country’s protective measures works well as a stacked bar, one per country.
Coefficients are best as horizontal bars with confidence interval whiskers to convey precision.
Top sectors across two periods side-by-side shows the shift to electronics.
Simple bar chart with EMDE reference lines is clear on mobile.
Impulse response functions need a line chart with confidence bands to show the dynamic effect.
Grouped by country and quartile, this highlights the jobs paradox in a small bar chart.
Quintile bars for rural and urban are instantly decipherable.
Mirrors the consumption chart, reinforcing the pattern.
One bar per country with an EMDE average line clearly shows India’s gap.
Bars for import and export days alongside EMDE median lines.
Percentile ranks are best as bars with cohort medians for context.
Current vs concluded stacked or adjacent bars show the doubling.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Government actions that try to shape which industries grow, by protecting them from foreign competition, giving them subsidies, or buying their products. Think of it as the state picking and backing its champion sectors.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The entire page is about whether India’s version has worked.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Any new government rule or action that gives domestic firms an advantage over foreign ones. Examples: raising import duties, banning certain imports, requiring government agencies to buy local, or giving cash subsidies only to Indian producers.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The counts that show India’s surge come from this definition, and they count every measure equally, no matter how big its impact.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A big public database that tracks government policy changes affecting international trade. Researchers use it to count how many new protective measures each country introduces each year.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The entire surge narrative rests on this dataset, and its counting rule (one ban equals one small subsidy tweak) is a crucial caveat.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Emerging market and developing economies: countries that are not yet fully wealthy but are not the poorest either. India, China, Brazil, Bangladesh are examples. Advanced economies (AEs) are the rich ones like the US, Germany, Japan.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Comparisons between India and the EMDE median ground the story in peer context.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Free trade agreement: a deal between countries to reduce tariffs on each other’s goods. Imagine a special market access card that lets your goods enter a partner’s country at a lower tax rate than goods from outsiders.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India’s FTAs with the EU and UK are the counterweight to its protectionist surge.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The actual tax rate a country charges on incoming goods at the border. Often lower than the maximum rate it has promised at the WTO. It is what a real importer pays, right now.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The 15.8% figure is India’s applied duty, the price wall its industrial policy puts between Indian consumers and foreign goods.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: When the government buys goods or services. From roads and bridges to stationery and laptops, the government is a massive shopper. Industrial policy turns that shopping list into a tool: prefer local suppliers, even if they are more expensive.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India’s distinctive use of procurement (23% of its protective measures) sets it apart from neighbors.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A government scheme that pays a cash bonus to manufacturers based on how much they produce. It is like a reward for making things in India, designed to attract big factories and global supply chains.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The PLI is India’s flagship industrial policy for electronics and other high-tech sectors, but it has disbursed only 12% of its budget.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A number that shows whether a country exports more of a product than the world average. A positive RCA means the country is relatively good at making that thing and sells a lot of it abroad.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The FTA tariff-cut chart uses RCA to see if India is committing to bigger tariff cuts in sectors where it is already strong or weak.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A World Bank score that measures how well the state machinery works: whether civil servants are competent, rules are predictable, and policies actually get implemented. High score means the government can get things done.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India’s 68th percentile score shows its bureaucracy is decent, but the gap to rich countries (88th) is where industrial policy stumbles.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A range around a statistical estimate that tells you how uncertain the number is. A wide interval means the true effect could be very different from the central estimate; a narrow one means we are fairly sure.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The export incentive effect has a confidence band from -51% to +87%, meaning we cannot say whether it works.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A number that shows how much one thing changes when another thing goes up by one unit. For example, a coefficient of 0.47 on import share means that a 1-percentage-point higher import share predicts 0.47 more protective measures.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Used to show what drives India’s targeting of industries.

plannedCharts.title: India nearly doubled its protective industrial policy measures
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The headline: India went from 125 to 239 protective measures a year, far above any other South Asian country and most EMDEs.

plannedCharts.title: The world is doing it too — a global protectionist wave
plannedCharts.subtitle: Global Trade Alert database via WB SAEU April 2026
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India is not alone. Industrial policy has surged worldwide since the pandemic, led by advanced economies.

plannedCharts.title: Where India sits among the big protectionist players
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India is the 6th most active country globally in protective industrial policy, and 3rd among EMDEs after China and Brazil.

plannedCharts.title: India’s toolkit: procurement and subsidies, not just tariffs
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India uses a very different mix of industrial policy tools from its South Asian neighbours — heavy on procurement, lighter on import restrictions.

plannedCharts.title: Who India protects: high-wage sectors and large firms
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Contrary to the stereotype of protecting sunset industries, India directs more protection at manufacturing sectors with higher wages and larger, more productive firms.

plannedCharts.title: Which sectors wear the armour
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Manufacturing gets half of all protective measures. Within manufacturing, food and electronics lead, with electronics rising sharply in the 2020s.

plannedCharts.title: The tariff wall: India’s import duties vs the world
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Even as India opens up through FTAs, its average import duty of about 16% remains among the highest of any large economy.

plannedCharts.title: Trade defence cuts imports. Export incentives? Not so much.
plannedCharts.subtitle: WB SAEU April 2026, local projection estimates
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The policy scorecard: import-restricting measures do reduce imports significantly. Export-promoting measures show no clear effect.

plannedCharts.title: The jobs paradox: services create jobs but get no protection
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Manufacturing received half of all IP measures but accounts for only 14% of employment. Services, which generate most new jobs, received almost no targeted protection.

plannedCharts.title: The hidden tax: tariffs hurt Indian households
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The proposed FTA tariff cuts with the EU and UK would raise consumption for every Indian household, across all income levels.

plannedCharts.title: Real incomes rise too, especially for the poorest
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The same story through income: tariff cuts raise real incomes across all households.

plannedCharts.title: Fiscal space is tight
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Industrial policy costs money, and India collects about 18% of GDP in tax — below the EMDE average of 20.4%.

plannedCharts.title: Customs clearance: India takes 3–4 times longer than EMDE peers
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Even well-designed industrial policy hits a wall if it takes weeks to clear goods through customs.

plannedCharts.title: Government effectiveness: India scores well, but far behind advanced economies
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India’s government effectiveness ranks in the 68th percentile globally — good for an EMDE, but the gap to the AE median (88th) is where implementation falls short.

plannedCharts.title: India is also opening up: FTA coverage set to double
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The counterweight: India’s new FTAs with the EU and UK will double preferential market access from 16% to 33% of global GDP.
